subject: Mathematics
title: Zara's Area Mystery
hook: Zara uses determinants to calculate land areas from coordinates, uncovering geometry hidden in numbers.

slides.title: Determinants
slides.storyContext: Zara's father is a land surveyor. He has coordinates of a triangular plot but needs its area. Determinants transform coordinates into area instantly.

slides.title: The Land Survey
slides.storyContext: Zara's father has a triangle plot with vertices at (0, 0), (4, 0), (2, 3) in a Delhi suburb. He's marked these with GPS. He asks Zara: what's the area? Dr. Mehra says: determinants give you the answer without the distance formula.

slides.title: What is a Determinant?
slides.storyContext: Dr. Mehra explains: A determinant is a special number calculated from a square matrix. It encodes information about the matrix's invertibility and geometric scaling.

points.label: Notation
points.text: For a square matrix A, determinant is det(A) or |A|.

points.label: 2×2 determinant
points.text: For A = [[a b], [c d]], det(A) = ad − bc.

points.label: Geometric meaning (2×2)
points.text: det(A) is the signed area of the parallelogram formed by row vectors (or column vectors) of A.

example.solution: det(A) = 2·4 − 3·1 = 8 − 3 = 5. The parallelogram formed by [2, 3] and [1, 4] has area 5.

slides.inSimpleWords: A determinant is a number derived from a square matrix. For 2×2, it's ad − bc.

slides.title: 3×3 Determinant (Expansion)
slides.storyContext: For Zara's triangle area, she needs a 3×3 determinant. Dr. Mehra teaches expansion by minors.

points.label: Expansion along row 1
points.text: For A = [[a b c], [d e f], [g h i]], det(A) = a(ei − fh) − b(di − fg) + c(dh − eg).

points.label: Minor
points.text: M_{ij} = determinant of 2×2 matrix after removing row i and column j.

points.label: Cofactor
points.text: C_{ij} = (−1)^{i+j} · M_{ij}. Alternating signs.

slides.inSimpleWords: Expand a 3×3 determinant by picking a row, then combine minors with alternating signs.

slides.title: Area of a Triangle from Coordinates
slides.storyContext: Zara's triangle has vertices A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(2, 3). Determinant gives area directly.

points.label: Formula
points.text: Area = (1/2) · |det of [[x₁ y₁ 1], [x₂ y₂ 1], [x₃ y₃ 1]]|.

points.label: Why it works
points.text: The determinant of this augmented matrix (with 1s) scales the area of the triangle by 2. Absolute value ensures positive area.

example.problem: Find area of triangle with vertices (0,0), (4,0), (2,3).

slides.inSimpleWords: Plug triangle vertices into a 3×3 determinant formula, divide by 2, take absolute value — instant area.

image.alt: Area of a Triangle from Coordinates — Determinants

slides.title: Properties of Determinants
slides.storyContext: Dr. Mehra shares rules that make calculations faster. Zara uses these shortcuts.

points.label: If two rows are identical
points.text: det(A) = 0. No unique area — degenerate shape.

points.label: If two rows are swapped
points.text: det changes sign. Order matters geometrically.

points.label: If a row is multiplied by k
points.text: det is multiplied by k. Scaling one side scales area by k.

points.label: Multiplicative property
points.text: det(A·B) = det(A)·det(B).

points.label: det(A^T) = det(A)
points.text: Transpose doesn't change determinant.

slides.inSimpleWords: These properties help simplify calculation. Identical rows mean zero area (degenerate). Swapping rows flips the sign.

slides.title: Cramer's Rule
slides.storyContext: Zara learns a powerful method to solve systems of linear equations using determinants — no inverse needed.

points.label: For 2 equations
points.text: a₁x + b₁y = c₁ and a₂x + b₂y = c₂. x = det([[c₁ b₁], [c₂ b₂]]) / det([[a₁ b₁], [a₂ b₂]]), y = det([[a₁ c₁], [a₂ c₂]]) / det([[a₁ b₁], [a₂ b₂]]).

points.label: General form
points.text: For system A·X = B, x_i = det(A_i) / det(A), where A_i is A with column i replaced by B.

points.label: Condition
points.text: Works only if det(A) ≠ 0 (unique solution exists).

example.problem: Solve 2x + 3y = 8 and x − y = 1 using Cramer's rule.

slides.inSimpleWords: Cramer's rule: replace columns one by one with the constants, calculate determinants, divide. Faster than matrix inverse for small systems.

slides.title: Collinearity Check
slides.storyContext: Zara's father marks three points on a map. Are they collinear (on a single line)? Determinant tells instantly.

points.label: Idea
points.text: Three points are collinear if and only if the area of the triangle they form is zero.

points.label: Method
points.text: Calculate det of [[x₁ y₁ 1], [x₂ y₂ 1], [x₃ y₃ 1]]. If det = 0, collinear.

slides.inSimpleWords: If three points' determinant is zero, they're on the same line.

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-plot Calculation
slides.storyContext: Zara's father surveyed 2 adjacent triangular plots. Plot 1: (0,0), (5,0), (2,4). Plot 2: (5,0), (8,0), (6.5,4). Find both areas and total.

example.problem: Calculate areas using determinants and find total.

slides.inSimpleWords: Apply the determinant area formula to each triangle separately, then sum.

slides.title: What Zara Learned
slides.storyContext: Determinants turned Zara into a math surveyor, solving land problems with elegance.

points.text: Determinant: a number from a square matrix. For 2×2: ad−bc.
3×3 determinant: expand by minors along a row, with alternating signs.
Geometric meaning: determinant = signed area (or volume in 3D) of parallelogram (or parallelepiped) formed by matrix rows/columns.
Triangle area = (1/2)|det([[x₁ y₁ 1], [x₂ y₂ 1], [x₃ y₃ 1]])|.
Cramer's rule: solve systems by replacing columns with constants, computing determinants, dividing.

slides.inSimpleWords: Determinants unlock geometry from coordinates. Instant areas, collinearity checks, system solutions.

subject: Mathematics
title: Priya's River Run
hook: Priya's morning run along a river teaches her about smooth curves, sudden breaks, and rates of change.

slides.title: Continuity and Differentiability
slides.storyContext: Priya runs along the Yamuna River. Some stretches are smooth; some have sudden drops (a wall). She realizes: smooth paths have good derivatives, broken paths do not.

slides.title: The River Path
slides.storyContext: Priya's running path elevation: flat for 1 km, then slopes up 45° for 2 km, then flat again. But there's a barrier wall (sudden 2-meter drop) that interrupts the path. The smooth slopes have good tangent lines; the wall breaks continuity.

slides.title: What is Continuity?
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Singh defines: A function f is continuous at x=c if the curve doesn't jump or break at that point.

points.label: Three conditions (all required)
points.text: 1) f(c) is defined. 2) lim_{x→c} f(x) exists. 3) lim_{x→c} f(x) = f(c).

points.label: Geometric intuition
points.text: You can draw the curve without lifting your pen.

points.label: Discontinuity types
points.text: Removable (hole at a point), jump (sudden jump), infinite (asymptote).

example.problem: Is f(x) = {x² if x≠1; 2 if x=1} continuous at x=1?
example.solution: f(1) = 2. lim_{x→1} x² = 1. Since limit ≠ f(1), discontinuous (removable discontinuity — the hole at (1,1) is not filled correctly).

slides.inSimpleWords: Continuous = no jumps, holes, or breaks. The limit from both sides equals the function value at that point.

slides.title: Introduction to Derivatives
slides.storyContext: Dev asks Priya: how fast were you running at the 2 km mark? The answer is the derivative — instantaneous rate of change.

points.label: Definition
points.text: Derivative of f at x=c: f'(c) = lim_{h→0} (f(c+h)−f(c)) / h.

points.label: Geometric meaning
points.text: Slope of the tangent line to the curve at (c, f(c)).

points.label: Notation
points.text: f'(x), df/dx, Df(x) all mean the same thing.

example.problem: Find derivative of f(x) = x² at x=3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative = rate of change, or slope of tangent line. Measures how fast the function is increasing/decreasing at that point.

slides.title: Rules for Derivatives (Power, Product, Chain)
slides.storyContext: Computing derivatives by definition is slow. Mrs. Singh teaches shortcut rules.

points.label: Power rule
points.text: d/dx [x^n] = n·x^{n-1}.

points.label: Product rule
points.text: d/dx [u·v] = u'·v + u·v'.

points.label: Quotient rule
points.text: d/dx [u/v] = (u'·v − u·v') / v².

slides.inSimpleWords: Power rule: power goes down, multiply. Product rule: first times derivative of second, plus second times derivative of first. Chain rule: derivative of outer times derivative of inner.

slides.title: Differentiability and Continuity
slides.storyContext: Mrs. Singh clarifies the relationship: If a function is differentiable (has a derivative), it must be continuous. But continuity doesn't guarantee differentiability.

points.label: Statement
points.text: If f is differentiable at x=c, then f is continuous at x=c.

points.label: Contrapositive
points.text: If f is discontinuous at x=c, then f is not differentiable at x=c.

points.label: Converse is false
points.text: f can be continuous but not differentiable. Example: f(x) = |x| at x=0 (sharp corner, no unique tangent).

example.solution: f is continuous at 0: lim_{x→0} |x| = 0 = f(0). But: left derivative = lim_{h→0⁻} (−h) / h = −1. Right derivative = lim_{h→0⁺} h / h = 1. Left ≠ Right, so not differentiable.

slides.inSimpleWords: Smooth curve (differentiable) ⟹ connected curve (continuous). But connected doesn't mean smooth — corners exist.

slides.title: Left and Right Derivatives
slides.storyContext: Priya's path has a sharp turn at the barrier wall. Dev explains left and right derivatives.

points.label: Left derivative
points.text: f'₋(c) = lim_{h→0⁻} (f(c+h)−f(c)) / h. Slope from the left.

points.label: Right derivative
points.text: f'₊(c) = lim_{h→0⁺} (f(c+h)−f(c)) / h. Slope from the right.

points.label: Differentiable iff
points.text: f'₋(c) = f'₊(c) and both exist.

example.problem: For f(x) = |x−2|, find left and right derivatives at x=2.
example.solution: f'₋(2) = −1 (slope from left is −1). f'₊(2) = 1 (slope from right is 1). Not differentiable at x=2 (sharp corner).

slides.inSimpleWords: Smooth functions have equal left and right slopes. Sharp corners have different slopes from each side.

slides.title: Instantaneous Velocity Problem
slides.storyContext: Priya's position at time t (in hours) is s(t) = t² (distance in km). What is her instantaneous velocity at t=2?

points.label: Position function
points.text: s(t) = t².

example.problem: Find instantaneous velocity at t=2 hours.
example.solution: v(2) = 2(2) = 4 km/hour. At the 2-hour mark, Priya is running at 4 km/hour.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative of position gives velocity. Tells you speed at a specific instant.

slides.title: Challenge: Piecewise Continuity and Differentiability
slides.storyContext: Priya's path function: f(x) = {x² if x < 1; 2x − 1 if x ≥ 1}. Is it continuous and differentiable at x=1?

example.problem: Check continuity and differentiability at x=1.
example.solution: Continuity: f(1) = 2(1)−1 = 1. lim_{x→1⁻} x² = 1. lim_{x→1⁺} (2x−1) = 1. All equal, so continuous. Differentiability: f'₋(1) = 2(1) = 2 (derivative of x²). f'₊(1) = 2 (derivative of 2x−1). Both equal, so differentiable.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check continuity at the junction (all pieces meet). Check if left and right derivatives match. If yes to both, smooth transition.

slides.title: What Priya Learned
slides.storyContext: Calculus explains the smoothness and speed of Priya's running path and any motion.

points.text: Continuity: no jumps, holes, or breaks. Three conditions: f(c) defined, limit exists, limit = f(c).
Derivative: instantaneous rate of change, slope of tangent line. f'(c) = lim_{h→0} (f(c+h)−f(c))/h.
Key rules: power, product, chain, quotient — shortcuts to compute derivatives without limits.
Differentiable ⟹ continuous. But continuous ≠ differentiable (corners break differentiability).
Sharp corners have unequal left/right derivatives. Smooth points have matching left/right derivatives.

slides.inSimpleWords: Continuous functions don't break. Differentiable functions are smooth. Derivatives measure instantaneous rate of change.

image.alt: What Priya Learned — Continuity and Differentiability

subject: Mathematics
title: Ananya's Business Optimization
hook: Ananya runs a small business making Indian snacks. Derivatives help her maximize profit and minimize waste.

slides.title: Application of Derivatives
slides.storyContext: Ananya's ladoo production factory gets x kilos of ghee per day. Profit depends on x. Too little ghee = low profit; too much = waste. Derivatives find the optimal x.

slides.title: The Ladoo Factory
slides.storyContext: Ananya's daily profit function: P(x) = −2x² + 100x − 500 (x = kilos of ghee, P = profit in rupees). Vikram says: derivatives find the maximum profit point. Where should she buy exactly the right amount of ghee?

slides.title: Critical Points and Extrema
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair teaches: To find max/min, take the derivative, set it to zero, solve for x.

points.label: Critical point
points.text: Point where f'(x) = 0 or f'(x) doesn't exist.

points.label: First Derivative Test
points.text: At x=c: if f' changes from + to −, it's a maximum. If − to +, it's a minimum. If no change, it's neither.

points.label: Second Derivative Test
points.text: If f''(c) > 0, c is a minimum. If f''(c) < 0, c is a maximum.

slides.inSimpleWords: Maximum = peak of a hill (derivative 0, second derivative negative). Minimum = valley (derivative 0, second derivative positive).

slides.title: Increasing and Decreasing Functions
slides.storyContext: Ananya checks: as x increases from 0, does profit grow or shrink? The sign of f'(x) tells.

points.label: f'(x) > 0
points.text: Function is increasing. Profit rises as ghee amount rises.

points.label: f'(x) < 0
points.text: Function is decreasing. Profit falls as ghee amount rises.

points.label: Finding intervals
points.text: Solve f'(x) = 0 to find critical points. Test signs of f' in each interval.

example.problem: For P(x) = −2x² + 100x − 500, find where it's increasing and decreasing.
example.solution: P'(x) = −4x + 100. P'(x) = 0 at x=25. For x < 25: P'(x) > 0 (increasing). For x > 25: P'(x) < 0 (decreasing). Max profit at x=25.

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative tells the direction: positive = up, negative = down, zero = flat (peak or valley).

slides.title: Concavity and Inflection Points
slides.storyContext: Prof. Nair introduces curvature: Does the curve bend upward (concave up) or downward (concave down)?

points.label: f''(x) > 0
points.text: Concave up. Graph looks like ⌢ (minimum at critical point).

points.label: f''(x) < 0
points.text: Concave down. Graph looks like ⌣ (maximum at critical point).

points.label: Inflection point
points.text: Where f''(x) = 0 and changes sign. Curve changes concavity.

example.problem: For f(x) = x³ − 3x² + 2, find inflection points.
example.solution: f'(x) = 3x² − 6x. f''(x) = 6x − 6. Set f''(x) = 0: 6x − 6 = 0 ⟹ x = 1. f''(0) = −6 < 0 (concave down left). f''(2) = 6 > 0 (concave up right). Inflection at x=1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Second derivative tells curvature. Zero and sign change = inflection point (curve flips from cup to cap).

slides.title: Optimization in Real Life
slides.storyContext: Vikram shares business scenarios where derivatives solve practical problems.

points.label: Minimize cost
points.text: Find dimensions of a packaging box that minimizes material (surface area) for fixed volume.

points.label: Maximize revenue
points.text: Find the price/quantity that maximizes profit = revenue − cost.

points.label: Minimize time
points.text: Find the optimal speed to minimize travel time + fuel cost.

slides.inSimpleWords: Set up function (cost, profit, time), take derivative, set to zero, solve. Second derivative confirms max or min.

slides.title: Box Optimization Problem
slides.storyContext: Ananya needs to ship ladoos in boxes. She has a rectangular sheet 20 cm × 30 cm. She'll cut squares of side x from corners, fold up, and tape. What x maximizes volume?
slides.inSimpleWords: Write volume in terms of x, find where derivative = 0, check which solution is in valid range, calculate max volume.

image.alt: Box Optimization Problem — Application of Derivatives

slides.title: Motion: Speed, Acceleration, Distance
slides.storyContext: Ananya's delivery bike position: s(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t (meters, t in seconds). What's instantaneous speed at t=2? Is the bike speeding up or slowing down?

points.label: Velocity = ds/dt
points.text: Speed at a moment.

points.label: Acceleration = dv/dt = d²s/dt²
points.text: How fast speed is changing.

example.problem: Find velocity and acceleration at t=2.
example.solution: v(t) = s'(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9. At t=2: v(2) = 12 − 24 + 9 = −3 m/s (moving backward). a(t) = v'(t) = 6t − 12. At t=2: a(2) = 12 − 12 = 0 m/s² (no acceleration at this instant).

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivative of position = velocity. Derivative of velocity = acceleration. Second derivative of position = acceleration.

slides.title: Challenge: Multi-step Optimization
slides.storyContext: Ananya sells ladoos at price p rupees per box. Daily demand q = 500 − 10p boxes. Cost per box is 20 rupees. Find price p that maximizes profit.
slides.inSimpleWords: Express profit as function of price/quantity, differentiate, set to zero, solve. Check second derivative for max/min.

slides.title: What Ananya Learned
slides.storyContext: Calculus turned Ananya into an optimizer, running her business with mathematical precision.

points.text: Critical points: f'(x) = 0. Find them to locate max/min.
First Derivative Test: derivative changes sign at critical point. + to − = max, − to + = min.
Second Derivative Test: f''(c) < 0 ⟹ max, f''(c) > 0 ⟹ min.
Concavity: f''(x) > 0 = concave up. f''(x) < 0 = concave down. Inflection = sign change of f''.
Real applications: optimize dimensions (volume, area), price (profit, revenue), motion (velocity, acceleration).

slides.inSimpleWords: Derivatives find where functions peak and valley. Critical business tool for profit, cost, and efficiency.
